Shipping Container Pool: Off-Grid Backyard Build Guide

How to convert a 40-foot high-cube container into a partially in-ground pool with a timber deck and solar-powered pump system.

Published10 min readUpdated 2026-10-06

Guide

What to know before you buy.

A decommissioned shipping container makes a structurally sound pool shell once the cut openings are reinforced and the interior is coated correctly. The steel structure, designed to stack six units high at sea, is massively overbuilt for a static in-ground application, which is what makes it structurally viable in the first place.

The critical step is the cut opening. Shipping containers derive their rigidity from the corrugated side panels — cut an opening without adding a steel frame header and the container will distort under load within a season. Before any cutting, weld a 100mm x 100mm RHS steel frame around the entire planned opening. This transfers the load path around the cut and keeps the container square.

The interior coating must be a marine-grade liner, not a painted surface. Paint lifts within a season when submerged. A spray-applied polyurea liner or a fitted vinyl liner anchored at the lip are the two options that hold long-term. Budget the liner as a significant fraction of the total project cost — it is not a place to economise.

Partial in-ground placement solves two problems: it reduces the visible height of the container above grade and it uses the surrounding soil as thermal mass to moderate water temperature. Excavate so the container sits with its floor at least 600mm below grade on the long sides, while the cut opening side remains accessible at deck level.

Power for the pump and lighting comes cleanly from a solar-charged portable power station inside the container. An EcoFlow Delta Pro 2 in a ventilated internal compartment, charged by a panel on the container roof, handles the circulation pump, LED strip lighting under the deck lip, and an outdoor shower without a grid connection.
